old: At its root sits a Latin word for reckoning or reasoning, dressed up with a simple 'toward' prefix.
It once simply meant 'to speak to' or 'to accuse' in a French-derived legal sense before English got hold of it.
Its silent extra letter, added in the 1500s by mistake, makes it a spelling cousin — sort of — of its doublet, 'areason.'
clues: This legal verb picked up a silent letter by mistake in the 1500s, when writers 'corrected' a spelling that never needed it. Its Old French ancestor meant to speak to or accuse someone in court.
It's not the same as indict: it's the courtroom step where a defendant stands before a judge, hears the formal charges read aloud, and enters a plea.
News reports say a suspect 'will be ___ed on Monday.' Figuratively, it also means to condemn harshly, as when a columnist ___s a government's handling of a crisis.
reviewNote: Clue 1 said the Old French word 'simply meant to speak to someone', dropping the entry's 'or accuse in court'; rewrote with the entry's spelling-mistake fact.
